content:
Over the past few months, we’ve been tracking something quite interesting across buy side hiring in Hong Kong.

Together with our Risk, Finance and Operations team, we’ve pulled together a short piece on how hiring is actually evolving in 2026.

A few things stood out:
• Hiring is back, but it’s highly selective rather than volume driven
• Operations is currently the most active function across hedge funds and asset managers
• Risk hiring is becoming far more commercial, with firms prioritising profiles that can sit close to the investment side
• Finance roles are shifting towards governance, oversight and structure rather than just production
• Most mandates now come with a very specific reason behind them, not just headcount growth

What’s been most noticeable from our side is that mandates are becoming more complex and deliberate. Firms aren’t looking to build teams in the way they did previously.

Over the past year, I've been reviewing hiring trends and speaking with insurance leaders across Hong Kong. One theme has been consistent: while budgets remain under pressure, finding the right talent continues to be a major challenge.

𝗧𝗵𝗲 𝗱𝗮𝘁𝗮 𝗳𝗿𝗼𝗺 𝟮𝟬𝟮𝟱–𝟮𝟬𝟮𝟲 𝗵𝗶𝗴𝗵𝗹𝗶𝗴𝗵𝘁𝘀 𝘀𝗲𝘃𝗲𝗿𝗮𝗹 𝗸𝗲𝘆 𝘁𝗿𝗲𝗻𝗱𝘀:
✅ Transformation remains a priority, with focus shifting toward automation, data, efficiency, and business value creation.
✅ Actuarial, Risk, and Compliance continue to be among the most talent-constrained functions.
✅ Mid-management talent (Assistant Manager to Senior Manager level) remains one of the biggest bottlenecks across insurers.
✅ Hiring processes have become more selective, with greater emphasis on productivity, retention risk, and commercial impact.
✅ Candidates are evaluating opportunities on more than compensation alone. Areas such as leadership, development, flexibility, and meaningful work all matter.

One statistic stood out: Business Analysts within Projects & Transformation saw the largest salary band increase between 2025 and 2026 (+23.5%), reflecting strong demand for professionals who can bridge business, technology, and change.

𝗪𝗵𝗲𝗻 𝗱𝗶𝘀𝗰𝘂𝘀𝘀𝗶𝗻𝗴 𝘁𝗮𝗹𝗲𝗻𝘁 𝘀𝘁𝗿𝗮𝘁𝗲𝗴𝘆 𝘄𝗶𝘁𝗵 𝗶𝗻𝘀𝘂𝗿𝗲𝗿𝘀, 𝗺𝗼𝘀𝘁 𝗰𝗵𝗮𝗹𝗹𝗲𝗻𝗴𝗲𝘀 𝘁𝘆𝗽𝗶𝗰𝗮𝗹𝗹𝘆 𝗳𝗮𝗹𝗹 𝗶𝗻𝘁𝗼 𝗳𝗼𝘂𝗿 𝗮𝗿𝗲𝗮𝘀:

𝗜𝘀 𝗶𝗻𝘀𝘂𝗿𝗮𝗻𝗰𝗲 𝗼𝗳𝗳𝘀𝗵𝗼𝗿𝗶𝗻𝗴 𝗰𝗿𝗲𝗮𝘁𝗶𝗻𝗴 𝘁𝗼𝗺𝗼𝗿𝗿𝗼𝘄'𝘀 𝗰𝗮𝗽𝗮𝗯𝗶𝗹𝗶𝘁𝘆 𝗴𝗮𝗽?

Over the past 12 months, one topic has come up consistently in conversations with both insurance professionals and hiring managers.

𝗔𝘀 𝗺𝗼𝗿𝗲 𝘄𝗼𝗿𝗸 𝗺𝗼𝘃𝗲𝘀 𝘁𝗼 𝗹𝗼𝘄𝗲𝗿-𝗰𝗼𝘀𝘁 𝗱𝗲𝗹𝗶𝘃𝗲𝗿𝘆 𝗰𝗲𝗻𝘁𝗿𝗲𝘀, 𝗮𝗿𝗲 𝗶𝗻𝘀𝘂𝗿𝗲𝗿𝘀 𝘂𝗻𝗶𝗻𝘁𝗲𝗻𝘁𝗶𝗼𝗻𝗮𝗹𝗹𝘆 𝗰𝗿𝗲𝗮𝘁𝗶𝗻𝗴 𝘁𝗼𝗺𝗼𝗿𝗿𝗼𝘄'𝘀 𝗰𝗮𝗽𝗮𝗯𝗶𝗹𝗶𝘁𝘆 𝗴𝗮𝗽?

Many group insurers are offshoring activities such as reporting, PMO support, finance processing, testing and operations as part of broader cost optimisation strategies.

While the cost benefits are clear, several concerns keep emerging from conversations across the market:
🔹 Loss of business and regulatory knowledge
🔹 Knowledge transfer risks when experienced employees leave
🔹 Reduced agility during transformation programmes
🔹 Challenges managing stakeholders remotely
🔹 Retention concerns among remaining teams

At the same time, demand in Hong Kong is increasingly shifting towards professionals who can lead transformation, influence stakeholders and bridge business teams with offshore delivery centres.

𝗣𝗲𝗿𝗵𝗮𝗽𝘀 𝘁𝗵𝗲 𝗯𝗶𝗴𝗴𝗲𝘀𝘁 𝘀𝗵𝗶𝗳𝘁 𝗶𝘀𝗻'𝘁 𝗷𝗼𝗯𝘀 𝗹𝗲𝗮𝘃𝗶𝗻𝗴 𝗛𝗼𝗻𝗴 𝗞𝗼𝗻𝗴. 𝗜𝘁'𝘀 𝘁𝗵𝗲 𝗰𝗵𝗮𝗻𝗴𝗶𝗻𝗴 𝗻𝗮𝘁𝘂𝗿𝗲 𝗼𝗳 𝘁𝗵𝗲 𝗷𝗼𝗯𝘀 𝘁𝗵𝗮𝘁 𝗿𝗲𝗺𝗮𝗶𝗻.

The market appears to be moving away from hiring people to 𝗗𝗼 𝘁𝗵𝗲 𝘄𝗼𝗿𝗸 and towards hiring people to 𝗟𝗲𝗮𝗱 𝘁𝗵𝗲 𝘄𝗼𝗿𝗸.

What's your view? Is offshoring creating a future leadership and capability gap, or is it simply the next evolution of the insurance operating model?

• Finance roles are shifting towards governance, oversight and structure rather than just production
